title: What is your average time spent creating a game?
author: Kandescent
selftext:
Hi folks. I'm taking a crack at building a game for the first time using Codex as a lowly Plus user. My workflow is I have a window with ChatGPT open, where I laid out my entire idea, brainstormed a bit, then had it create a roadmap, which I then use to have it create prompts in phases that I then paste into Codex. I didn't think my idea was that ambitious, especially seeing what people "one shot," but it has taken me about 2 weeks of use, with me having taken advantage of resets and hitting my limit a few times. 

I'm not complaining as I'm enjoying learning the process. My main questions are is this normal? Am I not being as efficient as I should be? Should I just have Codex take a crack at the whole thing instead of building it piece by piece?

Thanks.

comments.author: butchiebags
comments.body:
I think it depends a lot on the type of game and the scope.

The 1-shot demos are fast and easy because they don’t have any depth, adding that depth can get really tedious and break things along the way, so I feel like there’s a diminishing return on scale and the bigger your game is, the harder it is to vibe code

I’m working on a pretty ambitious project at the scale of a full game with an endgame system, kinda like a Minecraft/Diablo mashup.  I’m about 4 months in and been spending a lot of time on the world, terrain, audio, assets, skills, gameplay systems first, have not really started on assets yet but built out systems that make it easier to iterate and “churn out” models, textures, skills, music, etc.  with little to no code, despite the game being 100% procedurally generated.  I’ve done this so that I can focus on the art side without just ai generating everything.  It’s also setting this up like its own game engine almost, and it all runs on unreal engine 5.8, but my workflow is more like I’m modding my own game through the code directly, the game has its own agent built in basically that lets me configure the many hundreds of config variables without having to write ini files directly.

At this point, a session for me is calling an orchestrator  skill I created that will assess bugs and features that I just log from in the game while I play, and it assesses those against all the outstanding plan docs, and then it spawns about 5 subagents that run across 2 pcs, and each agent will build and test, use screenshots to reproduce issues, then the orchestrator manages all the git worktrees and merges all the work into the main branch in the repo.  The orchestrator also tracks open decisions I need to rule on, so it’s more like I’m managing a team of developers.

replies.author: Sencha-Games
replies.body:
Hm, I'm creating a game engine from scratch with AI assistance. I wouldn't recommend doing it without technical authority. Even I'm pressed with difficult decisions sometimes and have to go down research rabbit holes.

But, even within the constraints of solutions like Unreal or Godot (or even ThreeJS!) you can still come up with workflows that make your game easier/faster to develop. My engine, for instance, come with level design tools that are optimized around me not moving my cursor in between menus and applications. That will allow me to create large, unique spaces within the engine itself in a matter of minutes rather than hours. 

Let's say you were building a Skyrim clone in Unreal Engine. Creating inventory items on its own isn't that big of a deal. But then, setting up the data assets around the inventory items and THEN getting them all in one consolidated source, along with tracking the instances? That would require filling out lots of spreadsheets. I would instead ask Claude or Codex to help architect a system/workflow that allows me one source from which I'd author those items.

comments.author: Robthejob14
comments.body:
I'm doing something similar. IDK if this efficient but here's my flow: create game idea project>create project instructions>create canonical .md files (master, vision, scope...etc)>create & test core loop>created new project called One Shot Engineering, so i can create the "perfect" one shot for codex>use the previously created .md files for sources for that project too (and more project instructions). Also, I have a labeling system to try to keep things organized (Guide Chat ##, Work Chat ##,  PROPOSED, DECIDED, REJECTED...etc) Its pretty in depth and time consuming and I absolutely love it. I intend to make the One Shot Engineer a universal kind of tool after i do this first project. OH! I almost forgot. I also had ChatGPT include a sort of teaching mechanism or whatever, in the project instructions. So it teaches me about the relevant topics as we build. It explains terms, concepts, reasoning etc. Basically What, When, How, Why and more. I totally identify with the feeling of wondering if I'm being efficient enough, if my workflow is "good enough", am I over engineering, or making things more complicated than they should be. But I just try to do what ChatGPT suggests regarding things I have little knowledge in (game/app design) while checking my work via research. Im brand new at this but it's something I've always wanted to do and now I am able to pursue my dreams. I agree that being thorough is probably the better path. Also, just using AI to help you in the first place is vastly improving the efficiency of probably ANY design work.   
I hope this helps! I hope to hear how things progress. If you come up some badass workflow, please share, Im always looking to improve!
